import { Aside, Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import SeqDiagram from '../../../components/SeqDiagram.astro';

Your app is live and people have data in it. This tutorial ships its next
release: a change to what it stores, tested against the state the shipped
release wrote, published, and rolled out to one instance and then to an
organization. It follows `apps/kv-store`, a string key-value store, which the
running example extends with the time each key was last written. "v1" and
"v2" here are two releases of *your* app (`1.0.0` and `2.0.0`), not versions
of the SDK.

## What an upgrade does

An upgrade switches an instance to another release's code and keeps its state.
It is one entry in the app's own log: from that index on, the leader runs the
new component against the keys the old one wrote, and nothing runs at the
switch ([Upgrades & migrations](/protocol/upgrades/) covers who may
upgrade and organization-wide runs).

<Aside type="caution" title="No migrations in this version">
  `calimero-sdk` has no `#[app::migrate]` and the node runs no migration
  during an upgrade: an upgrade that names one (`migrate`) is refused
  (`MigrationsNotSupported`, below). The new code reads what the old code
  stored, so a release changes its state by adding to it, never by rewriting
  it in place ([Upgrades & state](/build/migrations/)).
</Aside>

So the work of shipping v2 is in three places: the state change has to be one
the new code can read alongside the old, a test has to prove it on real old
state, and the rollout has to get past the cluster's checks.

## 1. Keep the release you shipped

The state your users have was written by the bundle you published, so that
bundle is what the test runs. Commit it beside the crate the day you publish:

```bash
mkdir -p releases
cp dist/com.example.kv-store-1.0.0.mpk releases/1.0.0.mpk
```

`apps/kv-store/releases/0.1.0.mpk` is core's copy for the example app. Keep a
release's `.mpk` for as long as an instance may still run it.

## 2. Change the state

v1 keeps one map:

```rust
#[app::state(version = 1)]
pub struct KvStore {
    entries: UnorderedMap<String, String>,
}
```

v2 records when each key was last written. The safe change is a new field:
a new field is a new key range, empty until written, so v1's keys are where v2
looks for them and v2's new keys are where v1 never looked.

```rust
#[app::state(version = 2)]
pub struct KvStore {
    entries: UnorderedMap<String, String>,
    /// When each key was last written (ms); keys written by 1.0.0 have none.
    updated_at: UnorderedMap<String, u64>,
}

#[app::logic]
impl KvStore {
    pub fn set(&mut self, key: String, value: String) -> app::Result<()> {
        let _old = self.updated_at.insert(&key, &env::time_now())?;
        // .. as before
    }

    /// When `key` was last written, or `null` for a key 1.0.0 wrote and nothing since.
    #[app::view]
    pub fn updated_at(&self, key: String) -> app::Result<Option<u64>> {
        Ok(self.updated_at.get(&key)?)
    }
}
```

Bump `version` whenever the state's shape changes: it is in the ABI, and the
consent page shows the change to whoever approves the upgrade.

What v2 must not do is rename `entries`, change its key or value type, or
change a record's fields: the old rows would sit under the old name, or no
longer decode, and every call that reads them would fail or see nothing. When
a shape really has to change, **expand, then contract**: add the new field
beside the old one, have every write go to the new one (removing the key from
the old), have every read try the new one and then the old one, and remove the
old field only in a release after every instance has rewritten its data.

```rust
pub fn get(&self, key: String) -> app::Result<Option<Entry>> {
    if let Some(e) = self.records.get(&key)? {
        return Ok(Some(e));
    }
    Ok(self.entries.get(&key)?.map(Entry::from_v1))
}
```

## 3. Write the migration scenario

A migration scenario is an ordinary [scenario](/build/testing/#scenarios)
with one `{ "op": "upgrade" }` step: the steps before it run on the shipped
release and write state, the steps after it run on the build under test and
read it back. Saved variables (`"save"`) carry across the upgrade.

`migrations/1.0.0.json`:

```json
[
  { "as": "owner", "op": "call", "method": "set", "args": { "key": "a", "value": "1" } },
  { "as": "bob", "op": "call", "method": "set", "args": { "key": "gone", "value": "x" } },
  { "as": "owner", "op": "call", "method": "remove", "args": { "key": "gone" } },
  { "op": "upgrade" },
  { "as": "bob", "op": "view", "method": "entries", "args": {}, "expect": { "ok": { "a": "1" } } },
  { "as": "bob", "op": "view", "method": "updatedAt", "args": { "key": "a" }, "expect": { "ok": null } },
  { "as": "bob", "op": "call", "method": "set", "args": { "key": "a", "value": "2" } },
  { "as": "bob", "op": "view", "method": "len", "args": {}, "expect": { "ok": "1" } }
]
```

Test the paths users take: read what v1 wrote, overwrite it, delete it, and
read what v1 deleted. `migrations/1.0.0.org.json` names the organization, as
`scenarios/<name>.org.json` does.

`tests/migrations.rs` runs every file in `migrations/` against the matching
release (copy it from `apps/kv-store/tests/migrations.rs`):

```rust
use calimero_sdk::testing::{release_component, run_migration};

#[test]
fn every_release_upgrades_to_this_build() {
    let dir = Path::new(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR"));
    for path in common::scenarios_in(&dir.join("migrations")) {
        let version = path.file_stem().and_then(|s| s.to_str()).unwrap_or_default();
        let mpk = std::fs::read(dir.join("releases").join(format!("{version}.mpk"))).unwrap();
        let old = release_component(&mpk, None).unwrap();
        run_migration(&old, common::component(), common::org_of(&path), common::T0, &path)
            .unwrap_or_else(|e| panic!("{}: {e:#}", path.display()));
    }
}
```

with `calimero-sdk`'s `releases` feature on the dev-dependency
(`features = ["testing", "releases"]`). `release_component` checks the
bundle's signature and digest as a node does, so the test runs exactly the
code your users run.

## 4. Run it

```bash
cargo test --test migrations
```

A change v2 cannot read fails at the first step that reads it. Renaming
`entries` in the example app, for instance:

```text
migrations/0.1.0.json: step 5: {"as":"bob","method":"entries","op":"view",..}:
expected ok {"a":"1","b":"2"}, got Ok(Object {})
```

The data is still in the instance under the old name; v2 simply does not look
there. Fix the code, not the scenario.

<Aside type="tip">
  The harness runs the real component on the real engine, as
  [Testing apps](/build/testing/) describes. For node-level behaviour
  around an upgrade (who may approve it, an organization-wide run), a cluster
  scenario uses `deploy`, `install_package` and `upgrade_app`
  ([Testing strategy](/contribute/testing/#cluster-scenarios)).
</Aside>

## 5. Publish v2

Build, sign with **the same key** as v1 (another key makes another
application, not an upgrade) and publish, as in
[Packaging & signing](/build/packaging-signing/):

```bash
meroctl app build . --out kv-store.wasm
meroctl app pack --wasm kv-store.wasm --package com.example.kv-store \
  --app-version 2.0.0 --key my-signing-key.json --out dist/com.example.kv-store-2.0.0.mpk
cp dist/com.example.kv-store-2.0.0.mpk releases/2.0.0.mpk   # the next release tests against it
```

Add `--previous releases/1.0.0.mpk` to the `meroctl app pack` line and
it compares the ABI with the last release before signing: it warns
about changes that break callers and refuses a state change without a state
version bump ([App interface](/build/app-abi/#check-a-new-version-against-the-last)).

Then publish it to the cluster's registry
(`meroctl app publish dist/com.example.kv-store-2.0.0.mpk`); a node installs it
from there on the first upgrade that names it. A development cluster (`--dev`, as
`merod local` runs) also takes an upload:
`meroctl app install --path dist/com.example.kv-store-2.0.0.mpk`.

## 6. Upgrade one instance

Upgrade one instance first, yours or a test organization's, and use it:

<Steps>

1. Upgrade it. Whoever the package's manifest names approves with a passkey:
   the owner (or `MANAGE_APPLICATION` in its organization), or the publisher's
   holders for a `publisher` package.

   ```bash
   meroctl context update <app-id> --version 2.0.0 --dev-passkey ./dev-passkey.json
   ```

   This is `POST /apps/{app}/upgrade { version }`; the node answers
   `412 CONFIRM_REQUIRED` with a challenge over the target WASM's hash and the
   release's signed manifest. On a development cluster `--dev-passkey` signs
   it with the passkey file you logged in with; on a real cluster the owner
   approves in the console, or the app sends them to the node's consent page
   (`POST /consent/requests` with `kind: upgrade`), which shows the state
   version each side declares. From CI, an
   [upgrade key](/cloud/deploy-from-ci/) signs instead.

2. Check what it runs now: `meroctl context get <app-id>` shows the release,
   and `GET /auth/apps` (or `/orgs/{org}/apps`) the newer releases it may move
   to.

3. Call it. The reads your migration scenario made are the ones to try by
   hand: old keys read back, `updatedAt` is `null` for them until written.

</Steps>

## 7. Upgrade the organization

An organization-wide run upgrades every instance of the package in the
organization (or in one team, with `--cascade` its subtree) under one passkey
approval:

```bash
meroctl group upgrade trigger <org> --package com.example.kv-store --version 2.0.0 \
  --dev-passkey ./dev-passkey.json
meroctl group upgrade status <org> <run>
meroctl group upgrade retry <org> <run> --dev-passkey ./dev-passkey.json   # the failed instances, as a new run
```

The run (`POST /orgs/{org}/upgrade`, `GET /orgs/{org}/upgrades/{run}`) lists
the apps it targets, those `done` and, under `failed`, each failed app's
refusal. An app whose current component is the target's (a release that
changes only the frontend) is recorded on the new release without running
anything; a failure leaves that app on its release and the rest of the run
goes on. The operator runs the same
upgrade with `meroctl ops upgrade-namespace` where it holds app upgrades.

## Troubleshooting

In this version the node plans no migration from the two releases' ABIs:
every upgrade is code only
([What an upgrade runs](/protocol/upgrades/#what-an-upgrade-runs)). Each case
a migration plan would tell apart ends as follows.

| Case | What happens now | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Same state version | Code-only switch | Nothing |
| One version up | Code-only switch: no `#[app::migrate]` edge runs | Make the change additive (step 2) and prove it (step 3) |
| Down | Not refused: the code switches back and reads the state the newer release left | See [Rolling back](#rolling-back) |
| More than one version up | Not refused: a code-only switch | Test from every release still in use (one file per release in `migrations/`) |
| One up, no edge from the current version | Not refused: a code-only switch | As one version up |
| One side embeds an ABI and the other does not | Every component embeds its ABI | Nothing |
| The request names `migrate` | Refused: `422 UPGRADE_FAILED`, `details.error.code` `MigrationsNotSupported` | Leave `migrate` (`--migrate`) out |

The refusals an upgrade meets before it runs, and after:

| Refusal | Why | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `412 CONFIRM_REQUIRED` | The step-up: not an error | Approve with a passkey (`meroctl` does), or use an upgrade key |
| `403 FORBIDDEN` "upgrading this app needs whoever its package names" | The caller is not the owner, holds no `MANAGE_APPLICATION`, or is not the publisher's holder for a `publisher` package | Ask whoever the manifest's `upgrades` names |
| `403 FORBIDDEN` "decided by its operator" | The cluster's governance gives app upgrades to the operator | The operator upgrades (`POST /ops/apps/{app}/upgrade`) |
| `403 FORBIDDEN` "not moved to a release its publisher upgrades" | v1 is an `owner` release and v2 a `publisher` one | Keep `upgrades` as it was; a package moves only from `publisher` to `owner` |
| `409 CONFLICT` "no organization has bound its key yet" | A `publisher` package whose signing key no organization bound | Bind it: `POST /orgs/{org}/publishers` |
| `400 REJECTED` "unknown bundle" | A `bundle` hash the caller may not see, or not on the cluster | Name the release (`--version`), or install it first |
| `400 VERSION_REQUIRED` | An upgrade key named no version | Pass `--version` |
| `400 BAD_BUNDLE` | The release's component does not prepare on this node | Rebuild with the cluster's `calimero-sdk`; run `cargo test` first |
| `409 RELEASE_DEADLINE` | The organization whose approvals govern the app has approved no mero-tee release new enough, past the operator's deadline | Approve a current release on that organization (`namespace approve-release`; `account approve-release` does it on your personal organization) |
| `409 RUNTIME_TOO_OLD` | The release's `minRuntimeVersion` is newer than a replica's `merod` | Wait for the operator to roll the cluster, or build the release with a lower `--min-runtime-version` |
| `400 UNSUPPORTED_BUNDLE` | The target is a WASM core module (an SDK 0.12 build) | Rebuild with `meroctl app build` |
| `422 UPGRADE_FAILED`, `RUN_NEEDS_RESULT_METHOD` | A compute run in progress will call a result method v2 no longer declares | Keep the method in v2, or wait for the run to end |
| Calls fail or read nothing after the upgrade | v2 cannot read what v1 stored | Roll back, fix the state change, and add the case to `migrations/` |

## Rolling back

An upgrade back to the previous release is an upgrade like any other
(`meroctl context update <app-id> --version 1.0.0`), approved the same way. It
switches the code and keeps the state: whatever v2 wrote into its new fields
stays there, unread by v1, and is read again if v2 comes back. A v2 that wrote
into an old field in a shape v1 cannot decode is the one case a rollback does
not undo, which is why a release only ever adds fields.

## Several releases in use

An instance can skip releases, so v3 must read what v1 wrote as well as what
v2 wrote. Keep every release's `.mpk` and migration scenario while an instance
may still run it: `releases/1.0.0.mpk`, `releases/2.0.0.mpk`,
`migrations/1.0.0.json`, `migrations/2.0.0.json`, and the same test runs each
against the build. `GET /ops/apps` and `GET /orgs/{org}/apps` show which
release each instance runs, so you know when the last one moved and the old
field can go.
